extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of 19th‑century German history, literature, and arts; general educated public
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting evaluative standards and critical criteria used in a 19th‑century survey of German science, literature, and the arts — i.e., what the author treats as marks of good or bad practice in education, scholarship, poetry, architecture, painting, music, theatre, and social policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education of the lower classes (Pestalozzi)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pestalozzi chiefly encouraged the proper education of the lower classes and improved the method of instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schools were never neglected; immense improvements affected both the lowest popular schools and the colleges. Emphasis on practical improvements in instruction methods for the lower classes is treated as a central positive development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universities: political neutrality and broad promotion of sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: The universities... were, nevertheless, generally free from a political tendency and incredibly promoted the study of all the sciences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite surveillance and partial servile bias, universities should remain largely free from political tendency and foster all branches of science — this neutrality and breadth of promotion is praised as valuable for national progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shift from classical to national (German) studies
rubrics_metrics.description: The study of the classics... has been cast into the shade by the German studies, by the deeper investigation of the language, the law, the history of our forefathers and of the romantic Middle Age, by the great Catholic reaction, and... by the immense advance made in natural history, geography, and universal history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preference is given to investigation of national language, law, medieval heritage and scientific subjects over a narrow classical curriculum — a deeper, historically rooted national scholarship is presented as an advance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular style vs. concentrated representation in journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Every writer, almost without exception, affects a popular style. But, in this rich literary field, all springs up freely without connection or guidance. No party is concentrated or represented by any reigning journal... the immense number of journals published destroy each other's efficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proliferation of journals and ubiquitous popular style is criticized: diffuse, uncoordinated publication weakens sustained attention to important questions and dissipates influence; more cohesion or concentrated representation is implied as preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy should return to nature, history, and religion
rubrics_metrics.description: To him succeeded Schelling, with whom the return of philosophy to religion and that of abstract studies to nature and history commenced... It was a revival of the ancient mysticism...; nor was it unopposed... Abstract philosophy, despising nature and history, mocking Christianity, once more revived and set itself up as an absolute principle in Hegel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author praises philosophical approaches that reconnect abstract thought to nature, history and religion, and warns against purely abstract systems that ignore natural and historical realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science: empirical investigation plus practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: The discoveries of science were also zealously applied for practical uses. Agriculture, cattle‑breeding, manufactures received a fresh impulse and immense improvements as knowledge advanced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific work is valued both for theoretical discovery (astronomy, chemistry, natural history) and for tangible applications that improve agriculture, industry, commerce, medicine, and navigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philology and classics require Eastern/auxiliary language-study
rubrics_metrics.description: Even literati... have acknowledged that the knowledge of the Oriental tongues is requisite for the attainment of a thorough acquaintance with classic antiquity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thorough philological study should include Oriental languages and broader linguistic scholarship (also the study of ancient German) to achieve full understanding of classical antiquity and historic texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: History: impartial, source‑based scholarship
rubrics_metrics.description: The study of history became more profound and was extended over a wider field. A mass of archives hitherto secret were rendered public and spread new light... Historians also learned to compile with less party spirit and on more solid grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical writing is praised when it uses primary archives, eschews partisan bias, and compiles on solid, critical grounds rather than polemicism; critical source‑work (e.g., Pertz's plan) is a standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry: revival of older/national forms and simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: This school of poetry... owes its immense importance to its resuscitation of the older poetry of Germany... returned to the sacred simplicity of the ancient German and Italian masters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The romantic/national revival that recovers medieval German forms and simpler, older poetic modes (e.g., Minnesingers) is presented as a positive corrective to cosmopolitan frivolity and modern affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over‑refinement and effeminacy in poetic style
rubrics_metrics.description: Jean Paul Friedrich Richter... his clever but too deeply metaphysical romances are... full of domestic sentimentality... they also imitate the over‑refinement and effeminacy of Goethe...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive metaphysical refinement and effeminacy are criticized as faults; sound understanding and patriotism contrasted favorably with mere affected polish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cosmopolitan pastiche — preserve national stylistic integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Goethe and his school... have interwoven the most diverse strains, antique and romantic, old German and modern French, Grecian and Chinese, in one and the same poem. This unnatural style, itself destructive of the very peculiarity at which it aims...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mixing incompatible national and historical styles (pastiche) is condemned; authors and artists should preserve the peculiar character of the styles they adopt rather than fuse them indiscriminately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architecture: authenticity > eclectic mixing of styles
rubrics_metrics.description: the architect intermixes the Grecian and the Gothic in his creations... Architecture has... abandoned the periwig style of France, but the purer antique or Byzantine taste to which it has returned is generally insipidly simple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Architectural revival (e.g., Gothic) requires an elevated feeling and authentic understanding; mere eclectic mixing or insipid simplification is inadequate — authenticity and proper comprehension of style are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Painting: a middle path between slavish imitation and mere effect
rubrics_metrics.description: the two great schools at Munich and Dusseldorf... have sought a middle path, and with earnest zeal well and skilfully opposed the too narrow imitation of, and the medley of style produced by the study of, the numerous old masters on the one hand, and, on the other, the search for effect, that Gallic innovation so generally in vogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Painting should avoid both narrow imitation of old masters and a superficial search for sensational effect; a balanced, thoughtful approach that resists trends toward mere eclecticism or spectacle is advocated. Public commissions (church/state) would elevate painting's proper sphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music: preserve national musical character; avoid imitating licentious foreign opera
rubrics_metrics.description: In music, the Germans have retained their ancient fame... Still, much that is unnatural, affected, bizarre and licentious has crept into the compositions of the German masters, more particularly in the operas, owing to the imitation of the modern Italian and French composers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Musical composition should resist foreign imitations that introduce unnatural or licentious elements (especially in opera); popular choral practice (singing clubs) is praised as a corrective restoring national musical health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatre: should serve art/moral consolation, not be a political spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: The stage has most deeply degenerated... its mimic scenes afforded a species of consolation... The public afterward became so practical... the theatre became a mere political engine... intended to divert the thoughts of the population... by the all‑engrossing charms of actresses and ballet‑dancers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theatre ought to attract by the spirit of the actor and artistic merit rather than by coquetry, spectacle, or serving as political diversion; its degeneration into mere intrigue and low criticism is condemned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve beneficial customs when reforming social institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: The emancipation of the peasant... were indubitably well intended, but, instead of stopping there, good old customs, that ought only to have been freed from the weeds with which they had been overgrown, were totally eradicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social and legal reforms should remove abuses but preserve useful traditional institutions (e.g., inalienable allod, federal rights of the peasant); wholesale eradication of customs may produce unintended poverty and social dissolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support small trades/artificers via guild‑like protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional liberty and the introduction of mechanism and manufactural industry have annihilated every warrant formerly afforded by the artificer... Manufactures on an extensive scale... must at all events be left unrestricted, but the small trades...excite, when free, a degree of competition which is necessarily productive both of bad workmanship and poverty... The restoration of the city guilds under restrictions suitable to the times would have been far more judicious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small local trades require regulated protections adapted to modern times; unrestricted competition destroys craftsmanship and livelihoods — regulated guild structures (modernized) are recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charity vs. root‑cause social policy
rubrics_metrics.description: The public authorities throughout Germany have... displayed extraordinary solicitude for the poor by the foundation of charitable institutions... but they have contented themselves with merely alleviating misery instead of removing its causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public policy should go beyond charity to address causes of poverty: provide emigration avenues, secure peasant freehold, guarantee artificers' rights, maintain public morals, and avoid lax legislation that neutralizes moral sanctions.
